en.title: Luc Besson Would Only Make Terminator If It Cried About Its Mom
en.summary: The legendary French director Luc Besson shared his unique vision for a potential 'Terminator' film, emphasizing emotional depth over pure action. He also reflected on his early career freedom and his preference for exploring complex character dynamics.
en.body:
When asked about the possibility of helming a future installment in the iconic **Terminator** franchise, director **Luc Besson** offered a characteristically unconventional condition. Forget killer robots and time-traveling assassins; Besson’s version would hinge on a moment of profound vulnerability. "I like Schwarzenegger a lot, but I’d only make that film if the Terminator sat down and said he missed his mom," Besson quipped, revealing his disinterest in a straightforward continuation unless it offered a compelling, emotionally resonant angle.

This playful yet pointed remark underscores Besson's long-standing fascination with exploring the intricacies of human (and sometimes, non-human) emotion, particularly within the action genre he helped shape. He sees characters not just as plot devices but as complex beings wrestling with internal and external pressures. Besson has often gravitated towards stories that explore themes of "the strength of women and the weakness of men," and a Terminator that yearns for maternal connection certainly fits within this thematic playground.

## The Freedom of Early Cinema

Besson also touched upon the creative environment that allowed him to experiment and define his directorial voice in his earlier career. He rejects the notion that he single-handedly reinvented action cinema, instead crediting the freedom he experienced before the industry became heavily dominated by studio control and financial considerations. "When you don’t have a lot of experience, you have all this freedom," he explained. "You aren’t controlled by big studios and 50 people telling you why you can’t do something because it costs too much."

He lamented the current landscape where "people with money have taken control of cinema," asserting that "the one who decides is the creator." This perspective hints at a desire for artistic autonomy that fuels his distinctive filmmaking style, a style that has yielded classics like **Léon: The Professional** and **The Fifth Element**.

## A Director's Preferred Palette

Beyond his hypothetical franchise ambitions, Besson also singled out actors who have left a significant impression on him. He holds a deep admiration for performers who can embody the complex characters he enjoys crafting. Among those he named are **Gary Oldman**, known for his transformative roles; his ex-spouse **Milla Jovovich**, a frequent collaborator and star of **The Fifth Element** and **The Fifth Element**; and **Caleb Landry Jones**, who recently starred in Besson's film **Dogman**.

These actors, in their own ways, have demonstrated the ability to portray characters who are "always a little bit broken by society, always on the margins," aligning perfectly with Besson's thematic inclinations. His interest lies in the nuanced performances that can bring these flawed, compelling individuals to life, whether they are fighting aliens or contemplating their origins.

## What's Next

While a **Terminator** film helmed by **Luc Besson** remains a delightful "what if," fans can look forward to his ongoing contributions to cinema. His recent film **Dogman** has garnered attention for its unique narrative and **Caleb Landry Jones**'s performance, showcasing his continued commitment to character-driven stories with a distinct visual flair. Details regarding his next directorial project have not yet been announced.
